item.title: Cold Cases: Revisiting founding myths, iconic cases, and forgotten stories in management
item.content:encoded:
Anaïs Boutru, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Linda Rouleau, HEC Montréal

Géraldine Schmidt, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

Albéric Tellier, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Management research has long been populated by celebrated cases that have achieved the status of founding myths. Cases such as IBM's blindness to personal computing, Xerox's strategic myopia toward the graphical user interface, Nokia's fall to smartphones, the Mann Gulch fire, and Elton Mayo's Hawthorne experiments have become ubiquitous in the field's collective memory. These 'cold cases', endlessly cited and taught, structure ways of thinking and provide a shared foundation of representations that are central to the construction of epistemic communities.

Despite their pervasive influence, few studies scrutinize the empirical robustness, theoretical validity, or performativity of these emblematic cases. In management research, particularly in qualitative research, the risk of circularity is significant. Researchers working with inevitably heterogeneous and incomplete material may, even unconsciously, select data that confirm their theoretical priors, set aside disconfirming evidence, and ultimately favor demonstrations of the 'as if' type.

Appel publié par M@n@gement. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Reexamination and reinterpretation of canonical management cases (IBM, Xerox, Nokia, Kodak, Enron, etc.)
  • Empirical robustness and theoretical validity of emblematic cases in management scholarship
  • Performativity of famous cases and their role as epistemic artifacts
  • Processes of canonization and erasure in disciplinary memory
  • Circularity in qualitative management research and issues of confirmation bias
  • Role of founding myths in structuring management thinking and epistemic communities
  • Halo effects and the stratification of knowledge in management research
  • Forgotten cases and alternative narratives in management history
  • Critical reexamination of the Hawthorne experiments and other foundational studies
  • Replication, falsification, and verification in management research
  • Archaeology of management knowledge and disciplinary self-reflexivity

Timeline

  • October 14, 2026: Pre-submission workshop (online)
  • December 31, 2026: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Social change, backlash, and resistance in organizations
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Richard, Audencia Business School

Lucie Noury, Audencia Business School

Pauline de Becdelièvre, Université Paris Saclay

Céline Louche, Waikato Management School—University of Waikato

Stéphan Pezé, Université Toulouse Capitole

The production and dissemination of knowledge, particularly on inequalities, climate change, and biodiversity, are increasingly under attack. These attacks are reflected in some political and administrative decisions adopted across several national contexts, such as the measures taken by President Donald Trump since his return to power. Beyond the US, academic freedom is being directly or indirectly undermined in many countries. For example, in France, controversies surrounding 'Islamo-leftism' within universities, reignited by the Minister of Higher Education, have been accompanied by concrete attacks on several scientific institutions.

Appel publié par M@n@gement. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What are the different forms of backlash affecting organizations? Are there 'invisible' forms of backlash?
  • How and to what extent does backlash contribute to the deinstitutionalization of established norms (e.g. ESG, DEI, climate)?
  • What forms of institutional work produce or hinder backlash?
  • What roles do different modes of governance and different forms of organization play in weakening or, conversely, protecting social progress? Are democratic organizations, in particular, more or less prone to backlash?
  • How do organizations respond, resist, protect themselves, and participate in backlash?
  • What are the risks, uncertainties, and tensions generated by backlash? How can they be managed?
  • What forms of collective response are organized to face backlash (e.g. meta-organizations, networks, lobbying)?
  • How do individuals participate in or resist backlash (e.g. through employee activism)?
  • What is the impact of backlash on individuals (identity, career paths, values, social representations, experience)?
  • How does backlash transform or disrupt individuals' relationships with work and the company?
  • What forms of individual and collective resistance to backlash can be observed? What are the conditions and effects of this resistance?
  • What is the role of researchers and what stance should they adopt in response to this phenomenon?
  • What methodological and epistemological approaches are best suited to studying backlash, its mechanisms, and its consequences? What methodological innovations are needed to better understand its contemporary forms?
  • How can organizational theory contribute to understanding the phenomenon of backlash?
  • What are the multi-level interactions between societal, organizational, and individual backlash?
  • How can backlash contribute to the emergence of other backlashes?

Timeline
